name: Skillchirp
tagline: A skill-building product built around short structured practice sessions, with a thin public footprint.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The mechanical part of a practice app is genuinely small: a content model, a scheduler that decides what you see next, a streak counter, and a progress screen. An agent will hand you that in one sitting and it will work fine for one person. What it will not hand you is the curriculum, which is where products like this actually live or die, because a drill is only useful if someone competent decided it was the right drill in the right order. Public detail on Skillchirp is thin enough that the exact feature surface is unclear, so treat this as a verdict on the category rather than a line-by-line teardown. Build it if you already know what you want to practice; buy it if you want someone else to decide.
coreLoopDIY: A local app that stores your practice items, schedules the next one with spaced repetition, and tracks streaks and accuracy over time.
requirements: A local SQLite file, no server needed
Your own drill content in YAML, or an API key if you want the agent to draft it
whatYouLose: The authored curriculum: ordering, difficulty ramp, and knowing which drills are worth your time
Mobile: a localhost web app is not something you open in a queue at the shop
Push or email nudges, which are most of why habit apps work at all
Any social or accountability layer, if the product has one
Someone else fixing the content when it is wrong
moatNotes: Content is the product. The scheduling algorithm has been public since 1987 and is not defensible.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the hard part of practicing a skill is not tracking it, it is deciding what to practice next, and paying someone removes that decision. A self-built drill app tends to die the week you run out of drills you already knew you needed. There is also the nudge problem: a paid app can reach your phone at 8am, and your local Next.js project cannot, which quietly explains most of the retention gap between the two.
notes: Fully buildable shell, empty by default; the content you fill it with is the whole test.
prompt:
Build a local-first skill practice app called Drillbox. Single user, runs on my machine, no accounts.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS
- SQLite through better-sqlite3, file at ./data/drillbox.db, created and migrated on first boot
- No auth, no hosted services, no telemetry, no analytics

Content model:
- Drills are authored as YAML files in ./content/{skill}.yaml
- Each drill: id, prompt, answer, optional hint, optional tags, optional difficulty 1-5
- A loader parses ./content on startup and upserts drills into SQLite by id, so editing a YAML file and refreshing updates the drill without losing my review history
- Ship two example skill files with about ten drills each so the app is not empty on first run

Core loop:
- GET / shows today's queue: how many drills are due, a start button, current streak
- The session view shows one drill at a time, reveals the answer on click, then asks me to grade myself Again / Hard / Good / Easy
- Scheduling uses SM-2 spaced repetition, stored per drill: ease factor, interval in days, next due date, repetition count
- End of session shows a small summary: drills done, grade breakdown, next due date

Progress:
- /stats page with reviews per day for the last 60 days as a simple bar chart drawn with divs, not a chart library
- Per skill: total drills, drills seen, average ease, current streak

Explicitly out of scope: push notifications, email, mobile app, multi user, sharing, AI generation at runtime, deployment config.

Secrets: none needed. If you add anything optional that needs a key, read it from .env and commit a .env.example instead.

Deliver a README with setup in under five commands, a seed script, and one vitest file covering the SM-2 interval math.
